claims.claim: Diversification is the practice of spreading money among different investments to reduce risk: Investor.gov sums it up as 'don't put all your eggs in one basket', CFI describes it as allocating capital to a mix of different investments to reduce portfolio volatility, and OpenStax defines it as owning a variety of assets in a portfolio.

Diversification works because different investments often respond differently to the same conditions: factors that hurt one asset class or industry may help another, so gains in one holding can offset losses in another and smooth the overall result.

Diversification reduces the impact of firm-specific (unsystematic) risk — setbacks tied to a single company or industry, such as a product recall, weak management, or an industry-specific slump — because no single holding dominates the outcome.

Diversification cannot eliminate all risk: broad events such as recessions, interest-rate changes, and pandemics pull most investments down at the same time, and this systematic risk cannot be diversified away — portfolio risk falls with diversification but never reaches zero.

Diversification happens at three levels: across companies (many holdings instead of one), across industries (spreading holdings within an asset type), and across asset classes (different kinds of assets such as stocks, bonds, and cash).

The protection diversification provides depends on how much the holdings move together: combining holdings that respond to different conditions reduces a portfolio's swings more than combining similar ones, which is why many holdings in the same industry are not true diversification.

Adding holdings cuts risk most at the start: portfolio risk drops quickly as the first few holdings are added, and each further holding reduces risk by less — the benefit of spreading comes mostly from moving away from one holding.

Diversification trades away some upside for less downside: by holding many positions instead of one, an investor gives up the chance that a single winner produces a spectacular gain, in exchange for protection against a single failure being catastrophic; spreading money works in the hope that gains offset losses, not as a guarantee.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Investor.gov's glossary frames diversification as done 'in the hope' that gains in some investments make up for losses in others, while CFI and OpenStax frame it as a technique that measurably reduces portfolio volatility; the framings differ on how much certainty diversification provides.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the framings as complementary: diversification reduces the swings a portfolio experiences (the technique view) but is a hope, not a promise, that losses will be offset (the regulator's view). The honest note that diversification cannot remove all risk is supported by all three sources — OpenStax's systematic-risk floor, CFI's unsystematic/systematic distinction, and Investor.gov's 'hope' wording.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 15.2: Risk and Return to Multiple Assets
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook; aiIngestionAllowed:false per subject source-map). openstax.org blocks direct fetching, so the section was read via an Internet Archive capture (2024-09-15) on 2026-08-21. Supports: diversification as owning a variety of assets in a portfolio and the 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' framing; the $50,000 all-in-one-stock versus spread example; gains in one holding offsetting losses in another and washing away volatility; holdings that move together protecting less than holdings that respond to different conditions (airline versus oil example); portfolio risk dropping as holdings are added but never reaching zero because systematic risk cannot be eliminated; a portfolio concentrated in one industry (ten airlines) being not truly diversified. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: diversification as the practice of spreading money among different investments to reduce risk; allocating among different kinds of assets because conditions that hurt one asset class may improve another; spreading within each asset class across many stocks or bonds and across industry sectors such as consumer goods, health care, and technology; the warning that a narrowly focused fund, or several overlapping funds, may not provide real diversification. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Diversification (Investor.gov glossary)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator glossary). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: the working definition — diversification is a strategy summed up as 'don't put all your eggs in one basket,' spreading money among various investments in the hope that if one loses money, the others make up for those losses. The 'hope' framing supports the lesson's honest note that diversification reduces risk without promising gains. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

Supports: diversification as a technique of allocating capital to a mix of different investments to reduce portfolio volatility by offsetting losses in one asset class with gains in another; diversification primarily smoothing firm-specific (unsystematic) risk while leaving systematic market risk largely unaffected; balancing investments that have little positive correlation, or negative correlation; diversifying across asset classes, risk levels, and industries.
